Ruy Lopez (Closed): Castle kingside by move 5; Re1 and h3 support the center.
...b5 and ...d6 to kick the bishop, then ...Na5/...c5; the Marshall (...d5) is the sharp try.
Italian Game (Giuoco Pianissimo): Castle kingside by move 6, then build d3-c3 behind it.
...d5 to free the game, or ...Na5 to trade your bishop.
Scotch Game: Castle kingside quickly; the open center punishes delays.
Vienna Game: Castle before opening lines: f4 weakens your king.
...d5 to hit e4 and the center for quick equality.
Queen's Gambit: Castle kingside after Nf3/e3; focus on the queenside minority attack.
...c5 or ...e5 to free the position and escape the c4-d4 squeeze.
Catalan: Castle early; Bg2 shields the king.
...dxc4 and ...b5 to keep the pawn, or ...c5 to trade your center.
London System: Castle kingside after Bd3; e3/f2 form a safe shell.
...c5 + ...Qb6 hitting b2, ...Bf5 to trade bishops, or ...e5.
English Opening: ...e5 and ...d5 to take the center, or a symmetrical ...c5.
Reti / King's Indian Attack: Castle early, then attack the kingside with e4/e5.
...c5 and ...Nc6 hitting d4/e4, or a quick ...e5.
Alapin Sicilian (2.c3): Castle kingside after Be2; Black's play is on the other wing.
The ...d5 break to free the game and trade pieces.
Sicilian Najdorf: Castle kingside after ...Be7; if White castles long, race on the queenside.
Be3, Qd2, O-O-O and a g4-g5 or f4-f5 storm before your counterplay arrives.
Sicilian Dragon: Castle early; the g7 bishop and pawns are the shield, so avoid ...h6.
The Yugoslav Attack (Be3, f3, Qd2, O-O-O, h4-h5) to open the h-file.
French Defense: Castle after ...Be7; be ready for ...f5 or ...Qb6 against Bd3/Qg4.
Space with e5, a kingside attack, and keeping d4 protected.
Caro-Kann: Castle after ...Be7/...Nf6; counterplay starts on the queenside.
Space (e5 Advance) or h4-h5 + Bd3 kingside pressure; in the Panov, use the IQP.
Petroff Defense: Castle by move 7 and keep it simple.
Nc3 and Bd3 pressure for a small endgame edge; avoid a Qd2/Bh6 attack.
Ruy Lopez: Berlin Defense: The king walks to e8 or g8 after queens trade; ...Ke8 and ...h5 setups.
A pawn-structure endgame with the bishop pair; Black wants to keep it solid.
Scandinavian Defense: Tempo on the queen (Nc3, Bd2) and a lead in development.
Pirc Defense: Castle early behind the fianchetto; avoid ...h6.
A big center (e4-d4-f4) and Bc4/Be3/Qd2/h4 attack; counter with ...c5 or ...e5.
Queen's Gambit Declined: Castle early; free your light bishop with ...b6 or ...c5.
The minority attack or a c4-d4 squeeze; break with ...c5 or ...e5.
Slav / Semi-Slav: Castle after ...e6 and ...Be7; keep ...Bf5 outside the chain.
e4 to grab the center, a4 to hold c4; Black wants ...e5 or ...c5.
Nimzo-Indian: Castle after ...d5 or ...Bxc3; watch Bd3/Qc2 aiming at h7.
The bishop pair and a big center (e4, d4); Black hits e4 and keeps the c-file.
King's Indian Defense: Castle early, then ...f5 and ...g5; White often castles long.
Queenside expansion (c5), space, Bg5/h3 breaks and trading the g7 bishop.
Grunfeld Defense: A big center (c3-d4-e4) and kingside pressure; hold d4.
Dutch Defense (Leningrad / Stonewall): Castle early; watch the h4-e1 diagonal and e6.
Bg5, Nc3-b5, h4 and e4; take advantage of the e1-h4 diagonal.
Modern Benoni: Castle kingside; watch e4-e5, play ...Re8 and ...Nbd7.
The e4-e5 break, Bb5+, and restraining your queenside pawns.

sic.s: Asymmetry: White has the e-pawn and d-file play; Black has the half-open c-file and a d6/e6/g6 setup (Najdorf, Scheveningen, Dragon). Alapin and Rossolimo lines trade space for solidity.
sic.k: Both kings usually castle; with opposite-side castling, race with pawn storms (g4-g5 against ...b5-b4).
sic.p: White: bishops e3/e2/d3, knights d4/c3, queen d2. Black: Bg7/Be7, Rc8, knight c6/d7, queen c7/a5.
sic.pl: White attacks the kingside or exploits d5/e4 space; Black counterattacks on the queenside and the c-file and aims for ...d5.
sic.o: White wants a kingside attack before Black's counterplay; Black wants ...d5 or ...b5-b4 to open the position favorably.
sic.w: Nf3=develop and control d4;d4=open the center;Nxd4=central knight;Nc3=develop;Be3=English Attack setup;Qd2=connect, castle long;O-O-O=castle long, attack;f3=support e4 and g4;g4=kingside pawn storm;Be2=solid development;O-O=castle;c3=Alapin center
sic.b: Nc6=develop, hit d4;d6=support e5;Nf6=hit e4;a6=stop Nb5, prepare ...b5;e5=gain space;e6=solid Scheveningen;g6=Dragon fianchetto;Bg7=long diagonal;Be7=develop;O-O=castle;b5=queenside expansion;Rc8=c-file pressure;d5=central break;Qc7=flexible queen
sic.exp: Najdorf and Dragon structures were played by Fischer and Kasparov, among many others.
sic.why: The most popular reply to 1.e4: Black unbalances the game at once and plays for a win instead of mirroring White.
ideas: Black trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn: a queenside pawn majority and a half-open c-file.
White's lead in development and e4 space means Black must respect king attacks (Be3, Qd2, f3, g4).
Black's freeing breaks are ...d5 and ...b5; White's are e5, f4-f5 and Nd5.
Against Alapin and Closed lines, the fight is over the d4-d5 break and the center.
Sharp theory in Najdorf/Dragon; Scheveningen, Taimanov and Kan are more flexible.
Always count the race: pawn storm against your king versus counterplay on the c-file.
mist: Playing ...d5 early, before developing, so White's lead in development tells.
Ignoring White's kingside storm (g4-g5) while pushing ...b5 without support.
Memorizing sharp lines without the structure, then losing to a sideline.
trap: Bxf6 then Nd5 or e5 punishing a loose knight in 6.Bg5 lines (watch pins on d7/f6).
Nxe6 or Nd5 sacrifices when Black's king is uncastled and e6/d6 are loose.
sic.coach: Learn the structure before the moves. In the Najdorf, understand why ...a6 and ...e5/...e6 are played and what ...b5 and ...d5 achieve. Choose one Black system and one anti-Sicilian answer as White (Alapin is easiest to learn).
sic.end: Middlegames are double-edged; endgames favor the safer king and better pawn structure. Black's queenside majority is a long-term asset.
sic.mem: e4 vs c5: trade the c-pawn for the d-pawn, then Black strikes with ...d5 or ...b5 while White attacks the king.

french.s: Pawn chain e6/d5 against e5/d4 (Advance) or an open center (Exchange). Black's c8 bishop is the bad bishop; the d4/c3 base is the target for ...c5 and ...Qb6.
french.k: White usually castles kingside and attacks there; Black can castle either side but watch h7 and the f-file.
french.p: Black: knights c6/e7, Qb6/c7, trade the light bishop. White: Bd3, Nf3, Qd2, kingside space.
french.pl: Black hits d4 (...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6) and undermines e5 (...f6); White advances on the kingside or keeps the chain solid.
french.o: White wants space and a kingside attack; Black wants the ...c5 break and an active light bishop.
french.w: e5=gain space;Nc3=develop;Bd3=aim at the kingside;Nf3=develop;c3=support d4;Be2=solid;O-O=castle;Qd2=castle long ideas;f4=support e5;Bg5=pin Nf6
french.b: d5=challenge e4;c5=attack the d4 base;Nc6=pressure d4;Qb6=hit d4 and b2;f6=undermine e5;Nf6=develop;Be7=develop;Bd7=develop the bad bishop;O-O=castle;b6=free the light bishop;Bb4=Winawer pin
french.exp: Botvinnik and Korchnoi were famous French Defense players.
french.why: A solid, counter-punching defense: Black accepts a cramped position for a strong pawn chain and clear plans.
ideas: Attack the base of White's chain: ...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6 against d4.
Undermine e5 with ...f6 when White overextends.
Free the 'bad' light bishop with ...b6/...Ba6 or trade it.
White's plans are space, a kingside attack, or the Exchange for a quiet game.
The Winawer (3...Bb4) trades structure for activity and sharp play.
mist: Leaving the light bishop buried behind e6/d5 with no plan to free it.
Castling into a Bxh7+ or Qg4 attack without ...f5 or ...Qc7 defenses.
Letting White keep e5 and d4 both fully supported.
trap: Bxh7+ (Greek gift) after ...Nf6 and ...O-O with White's Ng5 and Qh5 ready.
Qg4 attacking g7 in the Winawer, when Black grabs pawns.
french.coach: Pick your structure (Classical, Advance, Tarrasch, Winawer) and learn its two or three key plans well. The French rewards patience: do not rush ...c5 before your pieces are ready, and always know how your light bishop gets out.
french.end: Endgames are often slightly better for White in the Exchange, but Black's solid structure and counterplay make the French hard to beat.
french.mem: e6, d5, then c5 and f6: hit the base of the chain and free the light bishop.

caro.s: Solid c6/d5 with a free light bishop (Classical) or a French-like chain (Advance). Black has no weaknesses and the endgame is comfortable.
caro.k: Black castles kingside after ...Be7 and ...Nf6; White's h-pawn push is the main king-attack idea.
caro.p: Black: Bf5/g6 outside the chain, Nd7/Nf6, Qc7. White: Nf3, Bd3, Bf4.
caro.pl: Black plays ...c5 or ...e5 to free the position; White uses space, or an IQP attack in the Panov.
caro.o: White wants a space edge and kingside pressure; Black wants safe development, then a pawn break.
caro.w: Nc3=develop;e5=gain space;Nf3=develop;Bd3=aim at the kingside;h4=attack the bishop;Bf4=develop actively;c3=support d4;O-O=castle;Qe2=flexible
caro.b: d5=challenge e4;dxe4=release tension;Bf5=develop outside the chain;Bg6=keep the bishop;e6=solid;Nf6=develop;Nd7=support;Qc7=flexible queen;Bd6=trade bishops;c5=break d4;Be7=develop;O-O=castle;h6=bishop retreat
caro.exp: Capablanca, Petrosian and Karpov are among the great Caro-Kann players.
caro.why: Rock-solid but not passive: Black keeps a healthy structure and a free light bishop and heads for a comfortable endgame.
ideas: Support d5 with c6, then develop the light bishop before ...e6.
Classical: ...Bf5, ...Nd7, ...Ngf6 and a safe, healthy structure.
Advance: attack the chain with ...c5 and ...Nc6 rather than waiting.
Panov: play for piece activity against the IQP.
Exchange: easy equality; use the half-open c-file.
mist: Playing ...e6 before the light bishop is out.
Pushing ...h6 and ...Bh7 without a plan against White's h4-h5 push.
Being too passive against the Advance Variation and getting squeezed.
trap: Nd6+ or Nxf7 tricks if the e-pawn is advanced and the king is stuck.
A Qa4 or Qb3 pin when Black's ...Bf5 hangs the b7 pawn.
caro.coach: The Caro-Kann is ideal if you like solid structures. Know your plan against each main reply: Advance (...c5, ...Bf5), Exchange (...Nc6, ...Bg4) and Classical (...Bf5 and ...e6). Aim for a safe middlegame and use the endgame edge.
caro.end: Endgames are Black's strength; White gets space but few targets.
caro.mem: c6, d5, free the bishop, then ...e6 and ...c5.

semi.s: Black avoids symmetrical development: a fianchetto (Pirc/Modern), a quick ...d5 (Scandinavian) or tempo play (Alekhine). White often gets a big center.
semi.k: Black castles short behind the fianchetto; White often attacks with f4/Be3/Qd2/h4.
semi.p: Black: Bg7, Nf6/Nd7, ...c5/...e5 breaks. White: Nc3, Nf3, Be3, Bc4.
semi.pl: Black waits, then undermines the center with ...c5 or ...e5; White consolidates the center and develops quickly.
semi.o: White wants a big center and a fast attack; Black wants to hit the center in time.
semi.b: Nf6=hit e4;g6=fianchetto;Bg7=long diagonal;d6=support;c6=support b5 and d5;Qa5=pin Nc3;Qd6=safe queen;O-O=castle;Bf5=develop;c5=counter the center;e5=challenge the center;Nc6=develop
semi.why: Hypermodern and semi-open defenses avoid book fights: Black lets White build, then counterattacks the center.
ideas: Black fianchettoes (Pirc/Modern) or hits e4 at once (Scandinavian, Alekhine).
White gets space and often a big center, but it can become a target.
Black's key breaks are ...c5, ...e5 and ...f5 at the right moment.
Develop quickly and avoid early queen moves unless they win time.
White should avoid overextension and keep pieces coordinated.
mist: Letting White roll forward with e5 and f4 without a counter-break.
Moving the queen repeatedly in the Scandinavian and falling behind in development.
Fianchettoing without castling early and leaving the king exposed.
trap: Bxf7+ or Bxh7+ if Black's king sits behind a fianchetto without defenders.
e5 forks or pins after Black ignores the center.
semi.coach: Know the move-order tricks: in the Pirc, White's Austrian Attack (f4) is the main danger; in the Scandinavian, learn the queen retreat squares (a5, d6, d8). Always counterattack the center within the first 8-10 moves.
semi.end: Black aims to undermine White's center and reach an equal middlegame with flexible pawn structure.
semi.mem: Let White build, then hit the center with ...c5 or ...e5.

ruy.s: Closed Spanish centre (e4/d3 or d4 against e5/d6) or an open centre after exd4. The b5 bishop pressures the knight that guards e5.
ruy.k: Both sides castle kingside early; the bishop and Re1 keep the center under control.
ruy.p: White: Bb3, Re1, knights d2-f1-g3. Black: Bb7, Re8, Na5/Nd7.
ruy.pl: White prepares c3-d4 and kingside maneuvers; Black expands with ...b5, ...Na5, ...c5 and ...d5.
ruy.o: White wants d4 at the right moment; Black wants ...d5 or queenside expansion and trades to ease the squeeze.
ruy.w: Bb5=pin the knight;Ba4=keep the pin;O-O=castle;Re1=support e4;c3=prepare d4;d4=central break;h3=prevent ...Bg4;Bb3=keep the bishop;Nbd2=reroute;Nf1=reroute;Ng3=kingside pressure;a4=hit b5;Bxc6=exchange variation
ruy.b: Nc6=defend e5;a6=question the bishop;Nf6=hit e4;Be7=develop;b5=gain space;d6=support e5;O-O=castle;Bb7=long diagonal;Re8=pressure e4;Na5=trade the bishop;c5=queenside play;d5=Marshall counter;Bc5=active bishop
ruy.exp: The Ruy Lopez has been a main weapon of Lasker, Capablanca, Fischer and Carlsen.
ruy.why: The classical main line of 1.e4 e5: slow pressure on e5 with endless middlegame plans and a small, lasting edge for White.
ideas: Bb5 pins the knight that defends e5; the real aim is long-term pressure on the center.
White builds c3 and d4 in the Closed Ruy, with Re1, Bb3 and h3 as standard moves.
Black expands with ...b5, ...Na5 and ...c5 or ...d5 breaks.
Exchange Variation: damaged queenside pawns for a healthier kingside majority.
Berlin Defense: a solid endgame-oriented defense; Marshall: a gambit for activity.
mist: Giving up the bishop on c6 without a plan for the resulting pawn structure.
Playing d4 before the center is supported (c3, Re1) and losing the e4 pawn.
Allowing ...d5 breaks without preparation in the Closed Ruy.
trap: The Marshall Gambit (...d5) is a deep, forcing line; know it or sidestep with 8.a4 (Anti-Marshall).
Bxc6 followed by Nxe5 winning a pawn when e5 loses its protector.
ruy.coach: Learn the closed structure: c3, d4, Nbd2-f1-g3 and the plans for both sides. Choose either the Main Line (Bb3, c3, h3) or the Exchange for a simpler game. If you dislike theory, play the Exchange.
ruy.end: Closed Ruy: slow maneuvering. Exchange and Berlin lines lead to endings where pawn structure and bishop pair decide.
ruy.mem: Bb5 pins; castle; Re1, c3, d4: build the center slowly and keep the e4 pawn safe.

italian.s: A flexible centre (c3/d3/e4) with the bishop on c4 eyeing f7. Often a slow, closed-ish structure where d4 is the central break.
italian.k: Castle kingside early; the bishop on c4 and the knight on f3 support play against f7.
italian.p: White: Bc4/b3, Nbd2-f1-g3, Re1, Qe2. Black: Bc5/Be7, Nc6, ...d6/...d5.
italian.pl: White builds with c3-d3, then d4 or a kingside regroup; Black frees the game with ...d5 or ...Na5.
italian.o: White wants d4 at the right time; Black wants ...d5 for equality or to trade the bishop.
italian.w: Nf3=develop;Bc4=aim at f7;c3=prepare d4;d3=solid center;O-O=castle;Re1=support e4;a4=stop ...b5;h3=stop ...Bg4;Nbd2=reroute;Nf1=reroute;Ng3=kingside pressure;d4=central break;b4=Evans gambit space;Bb3=keep the bishop
italian.b: Nc6=develop;Nf6=hit e4;Bc5=develop actively;Be7=solid;d6=support e5;O-O=castle;a6=prevent Bb5/Ba4 ideas;Ba7=keep the bishop;h6=stop Bg5;d5=central break;Na5=trade the bishop;Nxe4=take the e4 pawn
italian.why: A flexible, classical center-building opening aiming at f7, with little forced theory in the quiet Giuoco Pianissimo.
ideas: The bishop on c4 eyes f7; the center is built with c3, d3 and then d4.
Giuoco Pianissimo: slow maneuvering with a4, h3, Re1 and Nbd2-f1-g3.
Evans Gambit and Moller Attack give sharper play.
Black frees the game with ...d5 or ...Na5, or fights for e4 after Nf6.
Two Knights: avoid the Fried Liver theory with d3 (4.d3).
mist: Playing d4 too early without c3 support and losing the e4 pawn.
Retreating the bishop to b3 and then neglecting the center.
Falling for ...Nxe4 or ...d5 tactics when e4 is not defended.
trap: Fried Liver Attack (Nxf7) in the Two Knights after 4.Ng5 d5 5.exd5 Nxd5 6.Nxf7.
The ...Nxe4 trick when d3 has not been played and the Re1 pin disappears.
italian.coach: Aim for c3 and d3, castle, then reroute the knight to g3 or e3 and play d4 when the timing is right. Understand that this is a maneuvering opening: plan before you move.
italian.end: Often quiet and balanced; wins come from small advantages in pawn structure and piece activity.
italian.mem: Bc4, Nf3, c3, d3, O-O, Re1: then reroute the knight and strike with d4.

open.s: Open centre: lines open early, so development and king safety dominate. Structures range from open centres to gambit positions.
open.k: Castle early; do not leave the king in the center when lines open.
open.p: Develop knights then bishops; fight for the center and the f7/f2 squares.
open.pl: Complete development, castle, then open the center or attack the weak point.
open.o: The side with the initiative wants to open lines; the defender wants to neutralize with ...d5 or ...Nf6.
open.w: Nf3=develop;Nc3=develop;d4=central break;Bc4=aim at f7;Bd3=develop;O-O=castle;Be3=develop;f4=attack the center;Qe2=flexible;c3=prepare d4
open.b: Nc6=develop;Nf6=counter e4;d5=free the position;Be7=develop;Bc5=active bishop;O-O=castle;exd4=open the center;d6=support e5;Bg4=pin the knight
open.why: Classical open-game theory: rapid development, central tension and king safety decide the game.
ideas: Develop knights before bishops and castle early.
Fight for the center with d4 or ...d5 at the right moment.
Use gambit ideas (Scotch, King's Gambit, Vienna) only when you know the follow-up tactics.
Avoid pawn grabs that cost tempi; watch f7/f2 weaknesses.
Trade pieces when ahead; keep tension when your pieces are more active.
mist: Early queen sorties that lose time.
Leaving the king in the center when lines are open.
Grabbing a pawn and falling behind in development.
trap: Fried Liver, Legal's Mate and similar f7/f2 tactics.
Scholar's-style Qh5/Bc4 attacks on f7 if Black ignores them.
open.coach: Count your developed pieces versus your opponent's every move. If you are ahead, open the position; if behind, keep it closed or trade.
open.end: Open games reward activity; simplified endings depend on pawn structure and piece activity.
open.mem: Knights, bishops, castle, then open the center when ahead in development.

qg.s: c4/d4 against d5: Carlsbad (c6/e6), Slav chain (c6/d5), QGA (White regains c4), IQP or hanging pawns after exchanges. The minority attack (b4-b5) is White's key plan.
qg.k: Both sides castle kingside; the king is rarely attacked early.
qg.p: White: Bg5/Bf4, Nc3/Nf3, Bd3, Rc1. Black: Nbd7, Bb7 or Bf5, Be7, Rc8.
qg.pl: White: minority attack, e4 break or Bd3-Qc2 kingside play. Black: ...c5/...e5 breaks and trading light bishops.
qg.o: White wants e4 or a queenside attack; Black wants a pawn break (...c5/...e5) and active bishops.
qg.w: c4=attack d5;Nc3=develop;Nf3=develop;Bg5=pin Nf6;e3=support d4;Bd3=develop;O-O=castle;Qc2=flexible queen;Rc1=c-file pressure;cxd5=exchange, minority attack;b4=minority attack;e4=central break;Bxc4=regain the pawn;a3=prepare b4
qg.b: d5=hold the center;e6=solid;Nf6=develop;Be7=develop;O-O=castle;c6=Slav setup;dxc4=take the pawn;c5=free the position;Nbd7=develop;b6=Bb7 setup;Bb7=long diagonal;h6=ask the bishop;Ne4=trade pieces;Bf5=develop outside the chain
qg.exp: Capablanca and Karpov played the Queen's Gambit Declined with great success.
qg.why: The classical 1.d4 opening: White fights for e4 and the center; Black chooses solid structures (QGD, Slav) or active ones (QGA).
ideas: Challenge d5 with c4: if Black takes (QGA), White regains the pawn and gets center.
QGD: Black holds d5 with ...e6; the light bishop is the problem piece.
Slav: ...c6 keeps the light bishop free for ...Bf5.
Exchange Carlsbad: White plays the minority attack b4-b5; Black counters with ...Ne4 and ...f5.
Black's freeing moves are ...c5 and ...e5; White's are e4 and Qc2/Bd3 kingside play.
mist: Taking on c4 without a plan to hold the pawn (...b5) or return it.
Playing Bg5 too early or Nf3 too early without considering ...Ne4 or ...c5.
Ignoring the minority attack and allowing a permanently weak c6 pawn.
trap: Elephant Trap: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Nbd7 5.cxd5 exd5 6.Nxd5? Nxd5! 7.Bxd8 Bb4+ and Black wins.
Back-rank tactics when queens trade and the rooks are unconnected.
qg.coach: Know the three structures: Carlsbad (minority attack), IQP (attack vs blockade) and hanging pawns. Study the plans for each, then choose the QGD, Slav or QGA based on your style.
qg.end: QGD endings are usually balanced; Black's solid structure makes winning chances hard for White.
qg.mem: c4 vs d5: White takes the center, Black holds with e6 or c6 and breaks with ...c5.

indianQ.s: Black controls e4 with pieces (pin on c3 or Bb7) while White takes the c4/d4 centre or the bishop pair. Catalan: White uses g3/Bg2 pressure on d5 and the long diagonal.
indianQ.k: Kings castle short; Black often keeps a healthy pawn structure by giving up the bishop pair.
indianQ.p: Black: Bb4/Bb7 and the long diagonal. White: Nc3, Bd3, Qc2, e4 break; Catalan: Bg2, Qc2, Nbd2.
indianQ.pl: White occupies the centre with e4 or plays a3/Bxc3 structures; Black strikes with ...d5/...c5 and piece pressure.
indianQ.o: White wants the bishop pair and a big centre; Black wants to restrain e4 and hit the centre.
indianQ.w: d4=take the center;c4=space;Nc3=develop;Nf3=develop;g3=fianchetto;Bg2=long diagonal;O-O=castle;e3=solid;Bd3=develop;Qc2=flexible queen;a3=ask the Nimzo bishop;Bg5=pin;e4=central break
indianQ.b: Nf6=develop;e6=solid;Bb4=pin Nc3;b6=Queen's Indian;Bb7=long diagonal;O-O=castle;d5=central break;c5=counter in the center;Be7=develop;Bxc3=take the knight;Nc6=develop;d6=solid
indianQ.exp: Nimzowitsch (Nimzo-Indian), Karpov and Kramnik (Catalan) are strongly linked to these systems.
indianQ.why: Flexible, high-level systems: Black controls e4 with pieces; White fights with the bishop pair, the center or a fianchetto.
ideas: Nimzo: pin Nc3 and fight for e4; trade the bishop for knight to damage structure.
Queen's Indian: Bb7 and ...Be7 control e4 without weaknesses.
Catalan: use the long diagonal and queenside pressure.
Bogo-Indian: solid, flexible and low-risk for Black.
Plans revolve around e4, the c-file, and whether White gets the bishop pair.
mist: Giving up the bishop pair without compensation (Nimzo).
Playing ...d5 too early before the pieces are developed.
Letting White play e4 with a big center unopposed.
trap: Bxc3 followed by Ng5 or e4 winning the pinned knight if Black is careless.
Qa4+ forks after ...b5 in Catalan lines.
indianQ.coach: Learn the key structure: doubled c-pawns versus bishop pair (Nimzo), the long diagonal fight (Catalan) and the e4 break. Play solid, flexible moves and avoid early commitments.
indianQ.end: Balanced endgames with small edges decided by structure and bishops.
indianQ.mem: Control e4 with pieces, then break with ...d5 or ...c5.

kid.s: Hypermodern: Black fianchettoes and lets White build c4/d4/e4. KID: locked centre (d5/e5) with ...f5 against c5. Grünfeld: Black attacks the centre with pieces and ...c5. Benoni: asymmetrical with queenside majority.
kid.k: Black castles kingside and attacks it with pawns (...f5, ...g5) or keeps it solid; White often castles long to counter.
kid.p: Black: Bg7 (the monster), knights e8/d7/c6, rooks f8/e8. White: Be3/Bg5, Nf3, Qd2, space.
kid.pl: KID: ...e5 and ...f5 kingside play against White's c5/queenside space. Grünfeld: attack d4 with ...c5/...Nc6/...Bg4.
kid.o: White wants space and a queenside break; Black wants a kingside pawn storm or a central counterblow.
kid.b: Nf6=develop;g6=fianchetto;Bg7=long diagonal;d6=solid center;O-O=castle;e5=strike the center;c5=Benoni or Grunfeld break;Nc6=pressure d4;d5=Grunfeld counter;Nbd7=develop;Re8=pressure e4;Ne8=prepare ...f5;f5=kingside attack;Nxd5=Grunfeld capture
kid.exp: Fischer and Kasparov used the King's Indian Defense as a main weapon.
kid.why: Let White build a big center and attack it: dynamic, double-edged and rich in attacking chances for Black.
ideas: Black fianchettoes, castles, then strikes with ...e5 or ...c5.
Classical KID: after d5 the center locks; White plays on the queenside (c5), Black on the kingside (...f5-f4, ...g5).
Grünfeld: Black attacks the center with ...d5, ...Nxd5 and ...c5.
Benoni: asymmetrical; Black plays ...b5, ...Re8 and ...Nbd7.
The g7 bishop becomes a monster when the center closes.
mist: Pushing ...f5 before development is complete.
Allowing White's c5 break without counterplay.
Playing ...exd4 too early and giving White an easy central grip.
trap: Bg5 and Bxf6 followed by Nd5 when Black's knight leaves f6.
Early e5 pushes by White hitting the unprotected d6 pawn.
kid.coach: Learn the KID by structure: in the Classical, count the pawn storm race; in the Sämisch, the structure is different (...c5). Make sure you know your plan versus Bg5, h3 and f3 setups.
kid.end: Middlegames are sharp; endgames are less common, but a solid pawn structure and open g7 bishop help Black.
kid.mem: Fianchetto, castle, ...e5, ...f5: attack White's king while White attacks yours.

dutch.s: Black fights for e4 with ...f5: Stonewall (f5/e6/d5), Leningrad (g6/Bg7/d6) or Classical (d6/Be7).
dutch.k: Castle short, but the e1-h4 diagonal and the e6 square need care.
dutch.p: Black: Ne4 outpost, Bd6, Qe8-h5. White: Bg5/Bf4, Nc3, e3/e4.
dutch.pl: Black attacks the kingside with ...Ne4 and ...f4; White uses the weak e6 square and queenside play.
dutch.o: White wants to exploit the weakened king and e6; Black wants a kingside attack and control of e4.
dutch.b: f5=control e4;Nf6=develop;e6=Stonewall base;g6=Leningrad;Bg7=long diagonal;d5=Stonewall center;d6=Leningrad center;O-O=castle;Qe8=prepare ...Qh5;Ne4=outpost;Bd6=Stonewall bishop;c6=support d5
dutch.why: A fighting defense that claims e4 immediately and aims for kingside attacks, with a wide choice of structures.
ideas: Control e4 with ...f5 and develop the knight to f6.
Stonewall: pawns on f5/e6/d5 with an outpost on e4.
Leningrad: ...g6, ...Bg7 and a kingside pawn break with ...e5.
Classical: ...d6, ...Be7 and flexible play.
Watch the e1-h4 diagonal and the weak e6 square.
mist: Ignoring Bg5 and h4 attacks on the king.
Playing ...d5 too early in the Leningrad and losing the e4 outpost.
Allowing Nc3-b5 hits on c7.
trap: Bg5 and Nc3-b5-c7 forks when Black plays slowly.
Staunton Gambit (e4) tactics if Black grabs pawns without care.
dutch.coach: Choose your setup (Stonewall or Leningrad) and learn its plans. Be ready for White's Bg5, g3/Bg2 fianchetto and e4 break.
dutch.end: Complex middlegames; Black's king safety is the main issue.
dutch.mem: f5 controls e4: then Nf6, e6 or g6 and a kingside attack.

flank.s: Control d5/e5 with pieces and keep the centre flexible (Reversed Sicilian, Reti, King's Indian Attack). Transpositions are common.
flank.k: Castle short; g3/Bg2 is a safe shelter.
flank.p: Bg2 and Bb2 on the long diagonals, knights c3/f3, breaks with d4/e4.
flank.pl: Choose a centre after seeing Black's setup; expand with b4 or d4; attack with e4/Ne5.
flank.o: White wants a favourable centre; Black wants to claim the centre with ...e5/...d5 or symmetrical counterplay.
flank.w: c4=control d5;Nf3=develop;g3=fianchetto;Bg2=long diagonal;O-O=castle;Nc3=develop;d4=central break;b3=queen's bishop fianchetto;Bb2=long diagonal;e4=take the center;d3=solid;a3=prepare b4;b4=queenside expansion;Rb1=support b4
flank.b: e5=take the center;Nf6=develop;d5=hit c4;c5=symmetry and central pressure;g6=fianchetto;Bg7=long diagonal;Nc6=develop;e6=solid;Be7=develop;O-O=castle;d6=solid;Bb7=long diagonal
flank.why: Flexible flank openings control the center with pieces and avoid early theoretical battles.
ideas: Control d5 and e5 with pawns on c4 and pieces on f3 and c3.
Fianchetto the king's bishop (g3, Bg2) for long-diagonal pressure.
Choose a center after seeing Black's setup: d4 or e4.
Transpose to Queen's Gambit, Catalan or Sicilian-style structures.
English: reversed Sicilian ideas with extra tempo.
mist: Being too passive and letting Black take the center for free.
Playing d3 and e4 without a plan for the queenside pawns.
Neglecting development while chasing a fianchetto.
trap: Early Qb3 or Qa4 pins that win the c4 or d5 pawn if Black is careless.
Tactics on the long diagonal against b7/g7.
flank.coach: Flank openings are about flexibility, not speed. Make sure you know the main transpositions and what structures you want, then choose moves accordingly.
flank.end: Balanced, flexible endgames with minor advantages for the better-placed bishops.
flank.mem: Fianchetto, control d5 and e5, then pick the center.

qp.s: A compact pyramid (c3/d4/e3), fast development and flexible plans.
qp.k: Castle short; the king shelters behind e3/f2.
qp.pl: Complete the setup, castle, then Ne5/Qf3 or e4; against ...c5/...Qb6 trade or defend b2.
qp.o: White wants a safe fast setup and a kingside plan; Black wants ...c5/...Bf5 and an equal fight for the centre.
qp.w: d4=center;Bf4=London bishop;e3=solid center;c3=pyramid;Nf3=develop;Nbd2=develop;Bd3=aim at h7;O-O=castle;Ne5=outpost;Qb3=hit b7;Qf3=pressure;h3=keep the bishop;Bg5=pin
qp.b: d5=take the center;Nf6=develop;e6=solid;c5=challenge d4;Nc6=pressure d4;Bf5=develop outside the chain;Bd6=trade bishops;O-O=castle;Qb6=hit b2;Nh5=attack the bishop;Be7=develop;c6=solid
qp.why: Low-theory 1.d4 systems: a solid setup that you can reach against many Black replies.
ideas: Build a pyramid with c3, d4, e3, develop bishops outside the chain.
London: Bf4, e3, Nbd2, Bd3, Ne5.
Colle/Torre: Nbd2 with a quick e4 break.
Trompowsky: Bg5 at move 2, with a flexible, offbeat character.
Plans involve Ne5, f4 or e4 break, and kingside attacks.
mist: Playing the same setup without checking tactical issues (…Qb6, …Nh5, …Bf5).
Ignoring the c5/d4 tension and allowing ...Qb6 attacks on b2.
Trading pieces with no plan for your light-squared bishop.
trap: ...Qb6 hitting b2 after the bishop leaves the c1-h6 diagonal.
...Nh5 forks the bishop and f4/g3 squares when Bf4 is loose.
qp.coach: Solid is not automatic: learn the plan against ...c5/...Qb6, ...Bf5 and the King's Indian setups. Know when to switch to an e4 or c4 break.
qp.end: Equal-ish middlegames; success depends on planning, not memory.
qp.mem: c3, d4, e3, Bf4 or Bg5, then Ne5 and a kingside plan.
